title: Asked to sign off work you did not perform
situation: Your manager is behind on file review and asks you to sign the preparer sign-off on a working paper prepared by someone else — 'just sign it, I've looked at it, it's fine.' The paper supports a material balance.
principles_at_stake: Integrity; professional competence and due care.
code_reference: Code Part 1, s.110 (integrity; professional competence and due care); s.120 conceptual framework.
red_flags: ["Sign-off requested without review", "Material balance involved", "Verbal assurance instead of evidence", "Deadline pressure cited as justification"]
what_to_do: Politely decline and offer the honest alternative: review the paper properly first, then sign — or ask the actual preparer to sign. Document the request factually. If pressured, escalate to the engagement partner. A sign-off is a professional representation that you performed the work — signing blindly is a false statement.
what_not_to_do: Do not sign 'as a favour'. Do not backdate your sign-off. Do not assume the manager's verbal assurance transfers responsibility — it does not.
source_ref: CA Audit Intelligence Database — practice dilemmas (2026-10-23)

title: Backdating working papers to meet the assembly deadline
situation: The 60-day file assembly deadline has passed. Your manager asks you to date your completion working papers as if finished last week, 'so the file looks compliant.'
principles_at_stake: Integrity; professional behavior (conduct that discredits the profession).
red_flags: ["Explicit request to falsify a date", "Deadline already breached", "Framed as a paperwork formality"]
what_to_do: Date the papers with the actual completion date and document why assembly ran late. A late file with honest dates is a minor compliance point; a backdated file is dishonesty and, if discovered in a QCR or inspection, a career-damaging finding.
what_not_to_do: Do not backdate. Do not let anyone else backdate on your behalf.
source_ref: CA Audit Intelligence Database — practice dilemmas (2026-10-23)

title: Told not to book your real overtime hours
situation: You worked 70-hour weeks on an engagement. Your manager says 'don't book more than 45 hours — the budget can't take it, and it'll look bad on your evaluation.'
principles_at_stake: Integrity; professional competence and due care (accurate records underpin quality).
code_reference: Code Part 1, s.110; Part 2 considerations for employed members.
red_flags: ["Budget pressure overriding honest recording", "Evaluation used as leverage", "Systematic under-booking normalised in the team"]
what_to_do: Book your actual hours — time records are the basis for budgets, staffing and fee decisions, and falsifying them hides quality risk. If the culture punishes honesty, raise it with the engagement partner or HR; ICAP's training regulations expect trainees to be treated fairly.
what_not_to_do: Do not under-book to 'be a team player'. Chronic under-booking also masks understaffing that endangers audit quality.
source_ref: CA Audit Intelligence Database — practice dilemmas (2026-10-23)

title: Asked to keep bookkeeping work for an audit client quiet
situation: The firm prepares monthly bookkeeping for a small audit client. Your manager asks you to 'help out with their ledgers' and not mention it on the audit file — the client is also an audit client of the firm.
code_reference: Code Part 3 (members in practice); Part 4A (independence — self-review threat).
red_flags: ["Non-assurance service for an audit client", "Instruction to conceal it from the file", "You would later audit your own work"]
what_to_do: Decline the bookkeeping work for the audit client, or ensure it is properly evaluated for self-review threats with safeguards (separate teams, independent review) and documented. Concealing it is itself a breach — bring it to the engagement partner and the ethics partner.
what_not_to_do: Do not do the bookkeeping 'off the books'. Self-review threats cannot be managed by secrecy.
source_ref: CA Audit Intelligence Database — practice dilemmas (2026-10-23)

title: Manager says a found misstatement is 'too trivial to document'
situation: You found a Rs 800,000 error in a client's payables. Your manager says 'don't bother documenting it — it's clearly trivial, just tell them to fix it next year.' Overall materiality is Rs 5 million, but several similar items have already been waived.
principles_at_stake: Professional competence and due care; objectivity.
code_reference: Code Part 1, s.110; ISA 450 (accumulation of misstatements).
red_flags: ["Instruction not to document a finding", "Pattern of waived items accumulating", "Qualitative factors ignored (possible fraud indicator, covenant effect)"]
what_to_do: Document the misstatement and accumulate it per ISA 450 — individually immaterial items can be material in aggregate, and qualitative factors (fraud indicators, trends, covenants) can make a small amount material. Raise the pattern of waivers with the manager factually; escalate if dismissed.
what_not_to_do: Do not let findings disappear verbally. 'Trivial' is a documented judgement, not a conversation.
source_ref: CA Audit Intelligence Database — practice dilemmas (2026-10-23)

title: Management denies access to records or people
situation: The CFO says the warehouse manager 'is too busy' for your inventory inquiries, and withholds the related-party ledger 'until next week' — repeatedly. Fieldwork ends Friday.
principles_at_stake: Professional competence and due care; objectivity.
code_reference: Companies Act 2017 s.248 (auditor's right to information); ISA 500; ISA 705.
red_flags: ["Repeated delays targeting specific areas", "Gatekeeping of people, not just documents", "Deadlines used as leverage against you"]
what_to_do: Put the request in writing, citing s.248 of the Companies Act 2017 — the auditor has a statutory right of access at all times. Escalate to the engagement partner, then to TCWG. If access is still denied, it is a scope limitation: evaluate per ISA 705 (qualified opinion or disclaimer) and document everything.
what_not_to_do: Do not work around the limitation silently, and do not accept verbal summaries in place of the records.
source_ref: CA Audit Intelligence Database — practice dilemmas (2026-10-23)

title: Client offers gifts, hospitality or favours
situation: At the end of fieldwork the finance director gives the audit team expensive gift hampers and invites the manager to a family wedding with all expenses paid.
principles_at_stake: Objectivity; integrity; independence (familiarity and self-interest threats).
code_reference: Code Part 1, s.110; Part 4A (inducements, including gifts and hospitality).
red_flags: ["Value clearly more than trivial", "Timed at/after fieldwork", "Extended to families", "Offered by the people you are auditing"]
what_to_do: Decline anything beyond trivial, infrequent courtesies — and check the firm's policy, which is usually stricter than the Code. Disclose the offer to the engagement partner regardless. If in doubt, decline: the appearance of indebtedness damages objectivity even where none is intended.
what_not_to_do: Do not accept 'because everyone does'. Do not accept first and disclose later.
source_ref: CA Audit Intelligence Database — practice dilemmas (2026-10-23)

title: Pressure to accept management's estimate without challenge
situation: Management's ECL provision uses optimistic assumptions. The CFO says 'the board has approved it, the auditors last year accepted it, and we don't have time for another round.'
principles_at_stake: Objectivity; professional competence and due care; professional scepticism.
code_reference: Code Part 1, ss.110/120; ISA 540 (auditing accounting estimates).
red_flags: ["Appeal to prior-year acceptance", "Board approval presented as audit evidence", "Time pressure to stop challenging", "Assumptions consistently favourable"]
what_to_do: Challenge with evidence: develop your own range or point estimate, stress-test assumptions, inspect subsequent collection data. Board approval is not audit evidence. Document the challenge and management's responses; involve the engagement partner early.
what_not_to_do: Do not accept an estimate because challenging it is uncomfortable or slow. 'Last year accepted it' is not a procedure.
source_ref: CA Audit Intelligence Database — practice dilemmas (2026-10-23)

title: Asked to sit on a fraud indicator until after year-end
situation: You notice supplier payments to an unknown company with no purchase orders. The financial controller says 'let's not open this up now — mention it in the management letter after we close the audit.'
principles_at_stake: Integrity; professional behavior; responsibilities relating to fraud.
red_flags: ["Fraud indicator + request for delay", "Unknown vendor, no POs", "Management prefers the management letter to audit procedures"]
what_to_do: Treat it as a fraud risk indicator now, not later: extend procedures (vendor verification, payment tracing, related-party checks), inform the engagement partner immediately, and document. ISA 240 requires responses to fraud risks during the audit — deferral is not an option.
what_not_to_do: Do not agree to defer. Do not tip off the suspected individuals before the partner decides the approach.
source_ref: CA Audit Intelligence Database — practice dilemmas (2026-10-23)

title: 'Go easy on us — the bank loan depends on it'
situation: The CEO tells the engagement partner (within your hearing) that the company's Rs 200m loan renewal depends on 'a clean report without qualifications or emphasis paragraphs.'
code_reference: Code Part 1, ss.110/120 (intimidation threat); Part 4A; ISA 700.
red_flags: ["Outcome linked to the opinion", "Economic dependence leveraged", "Pressure applied in front of junior staff to normalise it"]
what_to_do: The opinion follows the evidence — never the client's financing needs. The engagement partner must make this clear to the CEO calmly and factually, document the conversation, and ensure the team is insulated. Evaluate whether the intimidation threat requires safeguards or withdrawal considerations.
what_not_to_do: Do not soften findings, skip procedures, or adjust materiality to 'help'. A clean opinion under pressure is worthless and dangerous.
source_ref: CA Audit Intelligence Database — practice dilemmas (2026-10-23)

title: TCWG member demands a specific audit outcome
situation: An influential board member (who is also a major shareholder) tells you privately that any qualification 'would destroy the share price' and asks you to 'find a way' to keep the report clean.
code_reference: Code Part 4A; ISA 260 (communication with TCWG — two-way, but the auditor decides the opinion).
red_flags: ["Private approach bypassing the engagement partner", "Share-price consequences invoked", "Request framed as loyalty to the company"]
what_to_do: Report the approach to the engagement partner immediately — this is itself a matter to document. The auditor's duty is to shareholders as a body and the public interest, not to any individual director. Communicate formally with TCWG as a body per ISA 260.
what_not_to_do: Do not negotiate the opinion. Do not keep the approach confidential from your partner.
source_ref: CA Audit Intelligence Database — practice dilemmas (2026-10-23)

title: Disagreement with TCWG over going-concern disclosure
situation: You conclude a material uncertainty exists. The audit committee chair insists the disclosure 'will become self-fulfilling' and refuses it, offering instead a private assurance that funding is arranged.
principles_at_stake: Professional competence and due care; integrity.
red_flags: ["Refusal of required disclosure", "Private assurances instead of evidence", "'Self-fulfilling prophecy' argument"]
what_to_do: Evaluate the funding evidence as you would any other: committed facilities, not assurances. If a material uncertainty exists, ISA 570 requires disclosure — its absence affects the opinion. Communicate the implications to TCWG in writing and document their response.
what_not_to_do: Do not accept private assurances as a substitute for disclosure. Do not let sympathy for the business override the reporting duty.
source_ref: CA Audit Intelligence Database — practice dilemmas (2026-10-23)

title: TCWG asks you not to put concerns in writing
situation: After you raise a significant deficiency in internal control, the chairman says 'we'll fix it — but please don't put it in the formal letter, it could leak.'
principles_at_stake: Professional competence and due care; integrity.
code_reference: ISA 265 (communicating deficiencies in internal control); ISA 260.
red_flags: ["Request to suppress required communication", "Leak fears used as justification", "Verbal-only handling of significant matters"]
what_to_do: Significant deficiencies must be communicated in writing to TCWG per ISA 265 — explain this calmly as a professional requirement, not a choice. Offer to discuss wording, but not existence, of the communication.
what_not_to_do: Do not agree to verbal-only communication of matters the standards require in writing.
source_ref: CA Audit Intelligence Database — practice dilemmas (2026-10-23)

title: ICAP Quality Control Review flags your engagement
situation: ICAP's QCR reviewer concludes your engagement file lacks sufficient documentation of the revenue work, and issues findings. Your partner is defensive and suggests 'the reviewer doesn't understand our approach.'
principles_at_stake: Professional competence and due care; professional behavior.
code_reference: ISQM 1 (firm quality management); Code Part 1, s.110.
red_flags: ["Defensiveness instead of root-cause analysis", "Blaming the reviewer", "Findings treated as a PR problem"]
what_to_do: Treat QCR findings as free consulting: perform a genuine root-cause analysis, remediate the file honestly (no backdating — see PD-TRN-02), and strengthen the firm's system of quality management. Cooperate fully and courteously with the reviewer.
what_not_to_do: Do not alter the file to 'fix' findings dishonestly. Do not dismiss findings without analysis.
source_ref: CA Audit Intelligence Database — practice dilemmas (2026-10-23)

title: SECP inquiry while bound by client confidentiality
situation: SECP writes to the firm seeking the audit working papers of a listed client under investigation. The client instructs you not to share anything, citing confidentiality.
principles_at_stake: Confidentiality vs. professional behavior and legal compliance.
code_reference: Code Part 1, s.110 (confidentiality — disclosure permitted/required by law); Companies Act provisions on regulator powers.
red_flags: ["Client instruction conflicting with legal duty", "Criminal/regulatory investigation context", "Pressure to obstruct"]
what_to_do: The Code permits — and sometimes requires — disclosure where there is a legal duty. Take legal advice, verify SECP's lawful authority for the request, inform the client of what the law requires, and comply with the lawful request. Document the legal basis for the disclosure.
what_not_to_do: Do not destroy, conceal or withhold documents from a lawful regulator request. Do not follow the client's instruction against the law.
source_ref: CA Audit Intelligence Database — practice dilemmas (2026-10-23)
